title: Expected vs realised move
teaches: Read the move the options market prices for a report (the implied move, quick-read from the at-the-money straddle), measure the move that really happened, divide one by the other, and say who was right and what a move far bigger than priced means for a holder.

facts.quote: Implied Volatility is a measure of how much the marketplace expects the asset price to move based on the price of the option.
facts.claim: Implied volatility is how far the market expects the price to move, read from option prices.

facts.quote: Statistical (Historical) Volatility is a measure of actual asset price changes over a specific period.
facts.claim: Historical volatility measures how much the price actually changed over a past period.

facts.quote: Implied volatility has no direct correlation to actual past historical or statistical volatility; rather it is a measure of predicted future movement.
facts.claim: Implied volatility is a forecast of future movement, not a record of past movement.

facts.quote: Implied volatility tends to increase when there is uncertainty or anticipated news, while it tends to decrease in times of calm.
facts.claim: Implied volatility tends to rise ahead of uncertainty or expected news and to fall when things calm down.

facts.quote: A decrease in implied volatility by 5% may result in the option losing around: .15 X 5 = $.75 in value.
facts.claim: All else equal, a drop in implied volatility takes value out of an option.

facts.quote: Higher volatility estimates indicate greater expected fluctuations (in either direction) in underlying price levels. This expectation generally results in higher option premiums for puts and calls alike.
facts.claim: A higher expected swing, in either direction, generally makes both calls and puts cost more.

facts.quote: A long straddle is a combination of buying a call and buying a put, both with the same strike price and expiration.
facts.claim: A straddle is a call and a put bought together at the same strike and expiry.

facts.quote: This strategy breaks even if, at expiration, the stock price is either above or below the strike price by the amount of premium paid.
facts.claim: At expiry, a straddle buyer breaks even only when the stock ends the full premium away from the strike.

facts.quote: The maximum loss is limited to the two premiums paid. The worst that can happen is for the stock price to hold steady and implied volatility to decline.
facts.claim: The straddle buyer's worst case is a stock that sits still while implied volatility falls.

facts.quote: This strategy involves selling a call option and a put option with the same expiration and strike price. It generally profits if the stock price and volatility remain steady.
facts.claim: The straddle seller generally profits when the stock and volatility stay steady.

facts.quote: The maximum gain is limited to the premiums received at the outset.
facts.claim: The straddle seller's best case is keeping the premium collected.

facts.quote: Review how implied volatility reflects the market's expectation of future stock movement and why it often falls sharply after earnings or other major announcements.
facts.claim: Implied volatility reflects expected movement, and it often falls sharply after earnings.

facts.quote: See how an option can lose value even when the stock moves in your favor
facts.claim: An option can lose value through an earnings report even when the stock moves your way.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: A triggered stop becomes a market order, and the fill can be far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Also, if you place your order before or after normal trading hours, consider the possibility that news events or other factors might significantly impact the price of the security when the market opens again.
facts.claim: News that lands outside the session can move the price a lot by the time the market opens again.

facts.quote: However, if markets are volatile and stock prices are changing rapidly, your stop order may be executed at a price that's significantly different from your stop price.
facts.claim: In a fast market a stop can fill well away from the stop price.

facts.quote: Immediately ahead of an earnings release, short-dated options prices reflect the market expectations of how a stock is likely to react.
facts.claim: Right before a report, short-dated option prices show the reaction the market expects.

facts.quote: The simplest way to estimate the magnitude of the reaction is by comparing the straddle price to historic moves.
facts.claim: Compare the straddle price with the stock's past reactions to size up the expected move.

facts.quote: Note that options pricing generally does not imply the direction of a reaction
facts.claim: Option prices generally do not say which way the stock will react.

facts.quote: just how much the stock is expected to move in either direction.
facts.claim: Option prices say how far the stock may move, up or down.

facts.quote: converted into an expected move using a 2/3 rule of thumb to estimate the highest probability point.
facts.claim: Cboe's note turned the implied standard deviation into an expected move with a two-thirds rule of thumb: one of several conventions.

facts.quote: strategies like straddles and strangles can profit from a large price move in either direction, provided the underlying's price move surpasses the total premium paid for the position.
facts.claim: A straddle profits from a big move either way only if the move beats the total premium paid.

facts.quote: Single stock options heading into earnings often carry high implied volatility, which inflates the premium on both calls and puts.
facts.claim: Into earnings, single-stock options often carry high implied volatility, which makes calls and puts pricier.

facts.quote: A trader buying a straddle on an individual stock may find that even a significant move in the stock doesn't cover the elevated cost of the options.
facts.claim: Even a big earnings move may not cover the high cost of a straddle.

facts.quote: Example A stock is trading at $200 ahead of earnings and the options market is implying a move of around 8% in either direction.
facts.claim: Cboe's example: a $200 stock with options implying about an 8% move either way.

facts.quote: And option traders would frequently use the price of a straddle as the expected move of a stock post-earnings event.
facts.claim: Option traders often use the straddle price as the expected move after earnings.

facts.quote: once that events comes and goes, the stock either moves by the expected move or more or it doesn't.
facts.claim: After the event the stock may move about as much as expected, more, or less.

facts.quote: it's not a determinant or determined factor that you could use with 100 percent accuracy.
facts.claim: The expected move is an estimate; it is not exact.

facts.quote: Historical volatility (HV) • Uses actual pricing data over the specified period • Measure of realized volatility
facts.claim: Historical volatility is built from the prices that actually printed: it measures realised volatility.

facts.quote: Long Straddle: Cost: $369 Maximum Gain = Unlimited Maximum Loss = $369 Results: Value: $0.04 + $2.77 = $2.81 * 100 shares = $281 Gain/Loss = $2.81 - $3.69 = $0.88 * 100 = $(88)
facts.claim: In Fidelity's earnings example, a straddle bought for $3.69 was worth $2.81 after the report: a loss of $88 per straddle.

facts.quote: Short Straddle: Credit: $354 Maximum Gain = $354 Maximum Loss = Unlimited Results: Value: $0.05 + $2.99 = $3.04 * 100 shares = $304 Gain/Loss = $3.54 - $3.04 = $0.54 * 100 = $54
facts.claim: In the same example, the straddle seller collected $3.54, bought it back for $3.04 and made $54 per straddle.

facts.quote: Volatility on the Calls: IV Mid was 92.88% with Vega at $0.0193 IV Mid ended up at 49.69% Option Value Lost due to Volatility = 92.88% - 49.69% = 43.19% * $0.0193 = about $0.83
facts.claim: In that example, implied volatility on the calls fell from 92.88% to 49.69% after the report, costing each call about $0.83.

facts.quote: The data used are from Wednesday, July 22, 2020, a few hours before the company's earnings release after the markets closed.
facts.claim: The MSFT example uses prices from July 22, 2020, hours before an after-the-close report.

facts.quote: Options markets signal the market's expectation for the stock's move after the earnings release.
facts.claim: Option prices signal the move the market expects after a report.

facts.quote: The simplest way to see that anticipated move is to look at the nearest term, at-money straddle.
facts.claim: The quickest read of the expected move is the nearest-expiry, at-the-money straddle.

facts.quote: The midpoint of those options, minus any intrinsic value, is a quick guide to the implied move of the stock.
facts.claim: The straddle's midpoint, less any intrinsic value, is a quick guide to the implied move.
MSFT's straddle priced a $9.48 move on a $209.58 stock: about 4.5%.

facts.quote: We noted that options markets were pricing in a move of about 6% for GOOGL, and the stock is up by just under that amount this morning.
facts.claim: GOOGL options priced about 6%, and the stock was up just under that the next morning.

facts.quote: For AMD, however, “only” a 7% move was priced in. It is currently about -10% lower.
facts.claim: AMD options priced about 7%, and the stock was about 10% lower the next morning.

facts.quote: Neither stock was pricing in a directional move, so the fact that we have one up and one down is not unexpected.
facts.claim: The options priced no direction for either stock, so one up and one down was no surprise.

facts.quote: Yesterday we highlighted options market expectations for Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)
facts.claim: The AMD and GOOGL expectations were written up the day before the October 30, 2024 post, ahead of their reports.

facts.quote: NVDA 1-Year Daily Candles with Arrows Pointing to the Days Following Prior Earnings Reports (November 20, 2024; February 26, 2025; May 28, 2025)
facts.claim: NVDA's three reports before August 2025 were on November 20, 2024, February 26, 2025 and May 28, 2025.

facts.quote: The most recent report led to a +3.25% gain
facts.claim: After its May 28, 2025 report, NVDA rose 3.25%.

facts.quote: The stock fell sharply (-8.48%) after the February 2025 report
facts.claim: After its February 2025 report, NVDA fell 8.48%.

facts.quote: It is also below the 7% that was expected last quarter, and the 8.4% that was priced in two quarters ago.
facts.claim: Options priced about 7% for NVDA's May 2025 report and about 8.4% for its February 2025 report.

facts.quote: At-money, near-term options are implying a roughly 6% post-earnings move for NVDA. That is below the 7.39% average of the stock's past 6 post-earnings moves
facts.claim: In August 2025 NVDA options priced about 6%, below the 7.39% average of its last six reactions.

facts.quote: As with AMZN, META's at-money, front-week options have an implied volatility of about 9%.
facts.claim: Before Meta's February 2024 report, its at-the-money front-week options implied about 9% for the day: the post's read of the priced move.

facts.quote: Meta's stock surged 20.3 per cent for the session, also recording its biggest one-day percentage increase in a year
facts.claim: Meta closed up 20.3% on February 2, 2024, the day after its report.

facts.claim: Earnings bring the risk of large gap moves.

facts.quote: So the stock is at 162 and a half and I'm going to look at the at-the-money or as close to at-the-money 162 and a half call and put.
facts.claim: Fidelity's live example: a $162.50 stock and the 162.50 strike call and put.

facts.quote: So one day to go, 162 and a half put and call is approximately trading for eight dollars and let's call it 30 cents.
facts.claim: With a day to expiry, that straddle traded for about $8.30.

walkthroughs.title: What the options are pricing
steps: Right before a report, short-dated options show how big a reaction the market expects. That's the implied move.
It's a size, not a direction. Options price how far, not which way.
The quick read: the at-the-money straddle in the nearest expiry. Call plus put, divided by the stock price.
Cboe's example: a $200 stock with options implying a move of about 8% either way.

walkthroughs.title: A real one: MSFT, July 2020
steps: MSFT, July 22, 2020, a few hours before its report. The stock is $209.58.
The straddle, less its intrinsic value, comes to $9.48. That's about 4.5% priced.
Other tools trim or scale the straddle, so their numbers differ a bit. Treat it as an estimate, never a promise.

walkthroughs.title: Implied vs realised
steps: After the report, measure what the stock actually did. That's the realised move.
Divide realised by implied. Near one is about as priced. Under one is smaller, over one is bigger.
GOOGL once priced about 6%, and the next morning it was up just under that. About as priced.
The straddle price is the hurdle. Bigger than priced pays the buyers. Smaller pays the sellers.

questions.q: Before a report, what does the stock's implied move tell you?
choices: How far options price it to move
How far it moved last time
questions.answer: How far options price it to move
questions.why: How far options price it to move. Right before a report, short-dated option prices show how big a reaction the market expects.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is the options market's estimate of the reaction's size.

wrong.Which way it should move: Options price a size, not a side. Up or down looks the same to the implied move.
wrong.How far it moved last time: That's history. You compare it with the implied move, but it isn't the implied move.
wrong.Where analysts see the price: Price targets come from analysts. The implied move comes from option prices.

questions.q: The implied move tells you which way the stock should go after the report.
questions.why: False. Option prices generally don't imply a direction, just how much the stock may move either way.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is a size. It says nothing about up or down.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ move is how far the stock actually went after the report.
questions.why: Realised. It's the move that actually happened. The implied move was the forecast made before it.
questions.lesson_line: Implied is the forecast. Realised is what the stock really did.

questions.q: Which options give the quickest read of the implied move?
choices: The call with the most volume
questions.why: The at-the-money straddle in the nearest expiry. Add the call and the put at the strike nearest the stock price. That total is the quick read.
questions.lesson_line: Nearest expiry, strike nearest the price, call plus put. That's your quick read.

wrong.Far out-of-the-money calls: Those only pay on a big move up. The at-the-money straddle prices a move either way.
wrong.The longest-dated puts: Long-dated options mix in months of other risk. You want the nearest expiry that covers the report.
wrong.The call with the most volume: Volume shows activity, not the priced move. Read the at-the-money straddle.

questions.q: A straddle buyer makes money at expiry as long as the stock moves.
questions.why: False. At expiry the buyer only breaks even when the stock ends the full premium away from the strike. A smaller move loses money.
questions.lesson_line: The straddle price is the hurdle. The move has to clear it.

questions.q: Implied volatility tends to rise ahead of known news like an earnings report.
questions.why: True. Implied volatility tends to climb into uncertainty or expected news, and single-stock options into earnings often carry high implied volatility.
questions.lesson_line: Into the report, options get pricier. That's the market paying up for the unknown.

questions.q: The report is out. What usually happens to implied volatility on the near-term options?
questions.why: It often falls sharply. Once the news is out, much of the uncertainty that was priced in is gone.
questions.lesson_line: The report removes the unknown. Implied volatility usually comes down with it.

wrong.It usually doubles: Rising is the build-up before the report. After it, implied volatility tends to drop.
wrong.It holds until expiry: It moves with supply and demand all the time. After a report it often falls right away.
wrong.It follows the stock's direction: Implied volatility measures expected size, not direction. It can fall after a big move up or down.

questions.q: Fill the blank with the right word.
questions.sentence: A straddle buyer needs the stock's move to beat the ___ paid.
questions.why: Premium. A straddle profits only if the move beats the total premium paid for the call and the put.
questions.lesson_line: Whatever the straddle costs, that's the move the buyer has to beat.

questions.q: The stock is $80. The at-the-money call and put cost $4.40 together. What move, in percent, is priced?
questions.why: 5.5%. The straddle divided by the stock price: $4.40 over $80.
questions.lesson_line: Straddle divided by price gives the implied move in percent. It's an estimate, not a promise.

questions.q: Its last close before the report was $80. Its first close after was $86.80. What was the realised move, in percent?
questions.why: 8.5%. The close after, minus the close before, divided by the close before.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the realised move from the last close before the report. Then hold it up against what was priced.

questions.q: Options priced a 4% move. The stock moved 10%. What is the realised move divided by the implied move?
questions.why: 2.5. The stock moved two and a half times what options priced. That's a real surprise.
questions.lesson_line: Realised over implied: under one is smaller than priced, over one is bigger.

questions.q: The implied move is the most a stock can move after the report.
questions.why: False. It's an estimate, and stocks can move more. AMD options once priced about 7%, and the next morning the stock was about 10% lower.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is a guide, not a ceiling. Plan for a bigger one.

questions.story: Options price a 5% move into the report. The stock gaps 12% and holds there into expiry.
questions.q: On the at-the-money straddle, who came out ahead?
questions.why: The straddle buyers. The move went well past the premium they paid, so the straddle is worth more than it cost.
questions.lesson_line: Bigger than priced pays the option buyers. Smaller than priced pays the sellers.

wrong.The straddle sellers: Sellers do well when the move stays inside the premium. A move far past it costs them.
wrong.Neither side, it's even: Even would need the move to land right at the premium paid. It went well past it.

questions.story: From a Fidelity options class: before a report, the at-the-money straddle cost $3.69. After the report it was worth $2.81.
questions.q: Who came out ahead on that straddle?
questions.why: The seller. The move didn't cover what the buyer paid, and implied volatility fell after the report. In Fidelity's example the buyer lost $88 a straddle and the seller made $54.
questions.lesson_line: A stock can move and the straddle still lose. The move has to beat what was paid.

wrong.The buyer: The straddle was worth less after the report than it cost. That's a loss for the buyer.
wrong.Both, since the stock moved: A move smaller than the premium hands the win to the seller. The buyer lost.

questions.q: NVDA, August 2025: options priced about 6%. Its last six reactions averaged 7.39%. What does that tell you?
choices: Options priced a smaller move than usual
Options priced a bigger move than usual
The stock will rise after the report
questions.answer: Options priced a smaller move than usual
questions.why: A smaller move than usual. About 6% priced against a 7.39% average for the last six reports. The market expected a calmer reaction than its history.
questions.lesson_line: Hold the implied move up against the stock's past reactions. That tells you if options expect a big one.

wrong.Options priced a bigger move than usual: 6% is below the 7.39% average, so it's smaller, not bigger.
wrong.The stock will rise after the report: The implied move has no direction. It can't tell you up or down.
wrong.The options are mispriced: Below average isn't wrong. The market can expect a quieter report than usual.

questions.q: After a report, implied volatility on the calls fell from 92.88% to 49.69%. All else equal, what did that do to the calls?
questions.why: Took value out of them. Lower implied volatility means lower premiums, all else equal. In Fidelity's example, that drop cost the call about $0.83 of premium.
questions.lesson_line: After the report, the volatility you paid for drains out. That's the volatility crush.

wrong.Added value to them: That's what rising implied volatility does. A fall does the opposite.
wrong.Nothing, only the stock matters: Implied volatility drives a big part of an option's price. A drop like this cuts the premium even if the stock holds still.

questions.story: NVDA reported on May 28, 2025. Options priced about a 7% move. The stock rose 3.25%.
questions.q: How did the realised move compare with what options priced?
questions.why: About 0.46x, smaller than priced. 3.25% against about 7% is less than half the move the market priced.
questions.lesson_line: A reaction well under the priced move tells you something too. The market braced for more than it got.

wrong.About 1x, right on the price: Right on would need a move near 7%. The stock moved 3.25%.
wrong.About 2x, far bigger than priced: That's backwards. The move was smaller than priced, not bigger.

questions.story: NVDA reported on February 26, 2025. Options priced about an 8.4% move. The stock fell 8.48%.
questions.q: Did options get the reaction right?
choices: Yes, the size was about as priced
No, it went down instead of up
No, it moved twice the priced move
questions.answer: Yes, the size was about as priced
questions.why: Yes, the size was about as priced. 8.48% against about 8.4% is almost exactly the move options expected. Direction was never part of the price.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the implied move on size. A big drop that matches the priced move is the market getting it right.

wrong.No, it went down instead of up: Options didn't price a direction. A fall of the priced size is right on.
wrong.No, it moved twice the priced move: Twice would be far more than 8.48%. It landed right about on 8.4%.

questions.q: Two websites can show different implied moves for the same report without either one being wrong.
questions.why: True. Some use the full straddle, some subtract intrinsic value, and Cboe's note scaled by a two-thirds rule of thumb. Know which method your tool uses.
questions.lesson_line: Check how your tool works out the implied move before you compare numbers across sites.

questions.story: AMD reported in late October 2024. Options priced about a 7% move. The next morning the stock was about 10% lower.
questions.q: How big was the reaction against what was priced?
questions.why: About 1.4x, bigger than priced. About 10% against about 7%. Bigger than the market expected, but well short of double.
questions.lesson_line: Read the ratio, not the headline. Bigger than priced, but not a shock.

wrong.About 0.7x, smaller than priced: That flips the ratio. Divide the realised move by the implied move, not the other way round.
wrong.About 1x, right on the price: Right on would be close to 7%. About 10% is clearly bigger.

questions.q: Meta, February 2024: front-week options implied about a 9% move. The stock closed up 20.3%. Realised divided by implied?
questions.why: 2.3. More than double the priced move. Reuters reported it as Meta's biggest one-day percentage gain in a year.
questions.lesson_line: Twice the priced move or more means the news landed far outside what the market priced.

questions.story: You own a stock into its report, which lands after the close. Your stop sits 4% below. Options price about a 9% move.
questions.q: What can your stop do for you overnight?
choices: Little, the open can gap right past it
Fill at the stop price on any gap
questions.answer: Little, the open can gap right past it
questions.why: Little. News outside the session can move the price a lot by the open, and a triggered stop becomes a market order that can fill far below your stop. A drop past 4% sits well inside the 9% the options priced.
questions.lesson_line: If the priced move is bigger than your stop, the stop isn't your risk. The gap is.

wrong.Cap the loss at 4%: A stop is a trigger, not a price. If the stock opens 9% lower, the sale happens near there.
wrong.Fill at the stop price on any gap: A triggered stop is a market order. On a gap it fills at the market, which can be far from your stop.

questions.q: You own 200 shares, last at $50 into the report, stop 4% below. It opens 9% lower and the stop fills there. What did the gap cost you?
questions.why: $900. 200 shares times $50 times 9%. That's more than double the 4% you planned to risk.
questions.lesson_line: Holding through a report, size for the gap the options price, not just for your stop.

questions.q: A stock moves twice its implied move after the report. What does that tell you?
choices: The news was far outside what was priced
The options were priced too high
The move will reverse the next day
questions.answer: The news was far outside what was priced
questions.why: The news was far outside what was priced. Options price the reaction the market expects. Twice that means the report surprised the market.
questions.lesson_line: Twice the priced move means the story changed. Note it, then judge the chart on its own merits.

wrong.The options were priced too high: Backwards. A move bigger than priced means the options were cheap for what happened.
wrong.The move will reverse the next day: Nothing in the implied move predicts tomorrow. Judge what happens next on its own.
wrong.Implied volatility will now rise: After a report, implied volatility usually falls, even after a big move.

conflicts: How the implied move is computed differs by source. Fidelity's 2022 class uses the full at-the-money straddle price; Interactive Brokers (Sosnick) subtracts any intrinsic value from the straddle midpoint; Cboe's Mag 7 note converts the implied standard deviation with a 2/3 rule of thumb; third-party tools (not cited) use 85% of the straddle. Our own earnings card (api/services/earnings_enrichment.get_implied_move) uses the full straddle divided by spot. The file teaches the full straddle as 'the quick read', calls every figure 'about', and q19 keys that two tools can differ without either being wrong.

q21 (Meta, February 2024): Sosnick's 'implied volatility of about 9%' is the daily implied volatility of the front-week at-the-money options, which he treats as the priced move (his 2020 post: daily IV and the straddle 'generally agree if the options are very short-lived'). A straddle-based figure would likely be somewhat lower, which only raises the ratio; 'more than double' holds either way. The question says 'implied about a 9% move', not 'the straddle priced 9%'.

Realised-move basis differs by source. Reuters' 20.3% (Meta) is the session close. Sosnick's AMD 'currently about -10% lower' and GOOGL 'up by just under that amount' are intraday the morning after (post at 1:00 pm, October 30, 2024); q20 says 'the next morning' and uses no close. His NVDA figures (+3.25%, -8.48%) are 'post-earnings moves'; the post does not say open or close. Every ratio is built from one writer's pair, never mixing bases.

MSFT, July 2020 (s14) is used only to read the implied move (9.48 / 209.58, about 4.5%). Its realised move is left out on purpose: the 209.58 base is an intraday price hours before the report, not the prior close, so a ratio against the next day's close (202.54) would mix bases.

s13's straddle example (2016 slides) does not name the stock; an earlier slide in the deck says 'The earnings date on this example is 2/25/16', but the slides never tie that date to the trade slides, so q14 gives no ticker and no date.

Cboe's insights posts are filed Tier 2 although cboe.com is listed under Tier 1 exchanges: they are research commentary, not a rule. Every key that cites them also cites a Tier 1 fact or a second Tier 2 publisher.
q20 says 'reported in late October 2024': the IBKR post (s15) is dated October 30, 2024 and says the AMD and GOOGL expectations were written up 'yesterday'; it does not state the report date itself.
